title: Capstone: incidents across the whole stack
tagline: One map from symptom to layer, the tradeoffs that keep coming back, and six incidents where the obvious cause is wrong.
why: Real incidents rarely stay inside one day's topic. A wrong answer from Relay can start in a cache, a replica, a job schedule, or an index long before the model sees anything. This day pulls the month into one procedure you can run under pressure, then makes you use it on incidents that cross layers and punish the first guess.
objectives: Classify an incident as error, slow, wrong, intermittent, or costly and name the cheapest evidence that narrows it to a layer
Separate the effects of two changes that shipped together before blaming either
Show whether an eval regression or a wrong answer came from infrastructure or from the model
Name which recurring tradeoff a design choice makes, and what it costs when the choice is wrong
Turn a fixed failure into a guard that runs: a test, an eval case, or an alert

lessons.title: The master map: from symptom to layer

blocks.text: Every incident reaches you as one of five symptoms: something errors, something is slow, something is wrong, something happens only sometimes, or something costs too much. Each symptom points to a short list of layers. Your first move is the cheapest piece of evidence that cuts that list in half.

Before any layer, ask the Day 6 question: what changed? In Relay, change comes from more places than code. A deploy, a config value, a migration, a job schedule, a model version, a prompt, an index rebuild, and a shift in traffic all count. Most incidents in this capstone begin with a change nobody connected to the symptom.

blocks.caption: Five symptoms and where each one points
rows: The status code and which hop emitted it
Proxy, app runtime, auth, a dependency
Reading app code for a 502 that nginx produced
One trace: which span holds the time
Database, pools, queue, LLM generation, retries
Adding hardware before finding the waiting span
Where the answer came from: cache, replica, retrieval, model
Cache, replica, index, retrieval, tools, prompt
Blaming the model when it never ran
What failing cases share: pod, time, version, key
One bad instance, races, replica lag, deploy skew
Retrying until it passes and calling it fixed
Calls and tokens per unit of work, by step
Retries, agent loops, cache misses, prompt growth
blocks.verdict: Classify first, then gather the evidence in the second column before touching anything. The wrong turns in the last column are all fixes applied before a layer was cleared.

steps.label: State the symptom precisely
steps.detail: Expected versus actual, for whom, since when, how often. 'Relay is broken' becomes 'refund answers quote 30 days since Tuesday'.
steps.fail: A vague symptom sends three people to three different layers.

steps.label: Ask what changed
steps.detail: Deploys, config, migrations, job schedules, model and prompt versions, index rebuilds, traffic.
steps.fail: When two changes ship together, the more visible one gets blamed.

steps.label: Find who emitted the error
steps.detail: The status code plus the proxy and app logs tell you which hop answered: load balancer, nginx, the API, or a dependency.
steps.fail: Debugging the app for an error the proxy generated.

steps.label: Follow one request by its ID
steps.detail: The waterfall shows which spans ran and how long each took. A missing span is evidence too.
steps.fail: Without a request ID you read averages and guess.

steps.label: Bisect with one experiment
steps.detail: Bypass the cache, pin the read to the primary, replay the prompt directly, run the old image. Each result clears or convicts a layer.
steps.fail: Changing two things at once makes the result unreadable.

steps.label: Mitigate, then fix and guard
steps.detail: Stop the harm first with a rollback, a flag, or a limit. Then fix the cause and add a test, an eval case, or an alert.
steps.fail: A mitigation mistaken for the fix leaves the cause waiting.

blocks.text: Wrong answers in a stack with a model in it

Wrong is the symptom most often blamed on the newest layer. In Relay, a wrong answer can come from a cached response, a lagging replica, a stale or half-built index, a retrieval miss, a tool that returned old data, or the model. Check them in the order the request touched them, and stop at the first one that was already wrong.

blocks.title: Relay's stack and how each layer lies

layers.name: Edge: load balancer, nginx
layers.role: Terminates connections and routes to API pods.
layers.breaks: Emits 502 or 504 itself, often during deploys or on long generations.

layers.name: API: FastAPI on uvicorn
layers.role: Runs handlers and calls everything else.
layers.breaks: A blocked event loop or an exhausted pool slows everything while CPU sits idle.

layers.name: Redis
layers.breaks: Stale or badly keyed entries serve wrong answers quickly; eviction drops sessions.

layers.name: PostgreSQL and pgvector
layers.breaks: Missing index, lock waits, replica lag, or a write half done.

layers.name: Queue and workers
layers.breaks: Redelivery runs a job twice; a backlog delays results; dead letters hide failures.

layers.name: LLM API
layers.breaks: 429s, overload, timeouts on long outputs, behavior change on a new version.

layers.name: Agent and eval harness
layers.role: Runs the tool loop and scores versions nightly.
layers.breaks: Tool results that mislead the model; infrastructure errors graded as model failures.

blocks.title: The newest layer gets blamed first
blocks.text: The model is the least familiar part of the stack, so it draws suspicion first. Many reports that the model got worse turn out to be a cache, a timeout, a rate limit, or an index that changed underneath it. Prove the model ran on the right inputs before judging its output.

blocks.title: Bypass, pin, replay
blocks.text: Three experiments settle most cross-layer questions. Bypass the cache and see if the answer changes. Pin the read to the primary and see if the data changes. Replay the exact prompt and retrieved context against the model and see if the output changes.

blocks.q: Relay's error rate is flat, but the LLM bill doubled overnight. What do you gather first?
options: LLM calls and tokens per ticket, split by step and by retry
The slow query log from PostgreSQL
Last night's eval scores by category
blocks.explain: A cost symptom with flat errors calls for counting the unit of cost per unit of work. That one breakdown shows whether calls multiplied (retries, loops) or each call grew (prompt or output length). The database and the eval do not bill tokens.

blocks.prompt: A trace for a wrong answer shows a Redis hit and then the reply, with no retrieval span and no LLM span. Which layers are cleared, and which one is now the suspect?
blocks.answer: Retrieval and the model are cleared for this request, because they never ran. The cached entry is the suspect: when it was written, what key it was stored under, and why nothing invalidated it when the content changed.

blocks.text: Over thirty days you met dozens of named tradeoffs. Nearly all of them are cases of six recurring tensions. Knowing which one you face tells you what you are paying, and what will break first if the choice turns out wrong.

blocks.caption: Six tensions behind most of the month's decisions
rows: Every reader sees the latest write
Waiting or refusing when a node or link fails
Fewer requests per machine, idle capacity
Harder to adapt to new needs
Less ability to handle the unexpected
blocks.verdict: Name the tension first, then the requirement that decides it. A choice made from a stated requirement survives review; a choice made from habit does not.

blocks.text: The same data can sit on both sides of one tension. Showing a customer their order status from a replica is fine; a few seconds of lag hurts nobody. Deciding whether to refund that order from the same replica is not fine, because the agent may act on a state that no longer exists. The requirement changed, so the choice changes.

options.name: Replica or cache
cost: An agent may act on old state
options.choose: Choose this for display and for decisions that tolerate a few seconds of staleness.

options.name: Primary
gain: Safe for decisions that move money
cost: A primary outage blocks the action
options.choose: Choose this for any read that decides a refund or another irreversible action.

blocks.text: Determinism against capability is the tension the AI half of Relay adds. A fixed workflow with code-enforced checks is easy to test and handles only what you planned. An agent handles odd tickets and fails in new ways. Relay mixes them: the model reads and writes language and proposes actions, and code enforces refund rules. Temperature 0 narrows variation but does not guarantee identical outputs.

Cost against quality and speed against safety travel together. Each cheaper option, such as a smaller model, a quantized one, or a cached answer, needs a measurement that would catch the quality it costs, broken down by category. Each faster release process needs a rollback that is faster still.

blocks.title: Every fix moves a cost somewhere
blocks.text: A cache moves cost into staleness. A retry moves it into load and duplicates. A queue moves it into delay and redelivery. An agent moves it into verification. When you adopt a fix, ask where the cost went and who will notice it first.

blocks.title: Choosing by habit
blocks.text: Always cache, always retry, and always use the bigger model are habits. Each was right somewhere this month and wrong somewhere else. Write the requirement next to the choice in the design note or the pull request, so the next person can tell when it stops holding.

blocks.q: Relay caches LLM answers to common help-center questions for 24 hours. What does this choice trade, and what does it cost?
options: Freshness for cost and latency; answers can go stale after content changes
Safety for speed of change; deploys become riskier
Capability for determinism; answers become less capable
blocks.explain: A cached answer is cheaper and faster than a fresh generation and is exactly as capable as the original. What it gives up is freshness: if the article changes, the cache keeps serving the old answer until the entry expires or is invalidated.

blocks.prompt: Relay's team wants to retry the payment call behind `issue_refund` automatically when it times out. Which tensions are involved, and what must be true first?
blocks.answer: Availability against correctness, and speed against safety. A timeout does not say whether the refund happened, so a blind retry can pay twice. Retrying is safe only with an idempotency key the payment provider honors, backoff with jitter, and a cap on attempts.

blocks.text: Debugging skill fades without practice, and real incidents are too rare to be your only practice. Four habits keep it sharp: postmortems for your own bugs, a debugging journal, reading other people's incident reports, and turning every failure into a check that runs.

items: Write a short postmortem for any bug that took more than an hour, even a local one: timeline, root cause, why it took so long, and one action.
Keep a debugging journal with one entry per hunt: symptom, first guess, evidence, actual cause, and time lost to the wrong guess.
Read one public incident report a week. Before reading the cause, write your own guess from the symptoms.
Turn every failure into a regression test, an eval case, or an alert, so the same bug cannot return quietly.

blocks.title: One debugging journal entry
blocks.code:
date:        2026-12-03
symptom:     customers logged out mid-chat, about 2 in 3 messages
first guess: Redis evicting session keys under memory pressure
evidence:    Redis memory 35%, zero evictions; logouts began with
             scale-out from 1 to 3 API pods; failing requests hit
             pods other than the one that created the session
cause:       new chat feature cached session data in process memory
time:        1h40m to root cause, 55m of it spent on Redis
faster path: ask what changed first; compare failing pod vs origin pod
guards:      CI test runs two API instances; review rule against
             module-level mutable caches in request handlers
notes: The first-guess line is the most valuable one. Over months it shows which layers you blame too early.
Time lost to the wrong guess measures the habit you are trying to improve, separately from the bug.
The entry ends with guards that run automatically. A lesson that lives only in the journal will be learned again the hard way.

blocks.caption: Four habits, compared
rows: Finding where your process failed, beyond the code
After any bug over an hour
Noticing which layers you suspect too early
Pattern recognition in systems you do not run
Making the system remember so you do not have to
blocks.verdict: If you keep only one habit, keep the journal. It is cheap, and the first-guess column is the fastest feedback on your own judgment.

blocks.text: Reuse the field guides. Every day of this course ended with a symptom-to-cause table. Rewrite the rows that matter for your project in your own words, add rows from your journal, and keep them somewhere you will find them at 2 a.m.

blocks.title: Where a fixed failure should live

options.name: Regression test
cost: Only covers behavior you can assert exactly
options.choose: Choose this when the failure is in code with one definite right answer.

options.name: Eval case
options.choose: Choose this when the failure is in what the model or agent decided.

options.name: Alert
options.choose: Choose this when the failure depends on live data, traffic, or a third party.

blocks.title: The postmortem that changes nothing
blocks.text: Action items like 'be more careful' or 'monitor closely' guarantee a repeat. Each action should be a specific change: a test, an eval case, an alert with a threshold, a config check in CI, or a sharp edge removed from the code.

blocks.title: Guess before you read
blocks.text: When you read an incident report or a drill, write down your guess and your first check before reading the cause. Comparing your guess with the answer is the practice. Reading the answer alone feels like learning and mostly is not.

blocks.q: Relay's agent once refunded an order outside the refund window. The bug is fixed. Where should this failure live so it cannot return unseen?
options: A policy check in code with a test, plus a case in the nightly eval
A new paragraph in the system prompt about refund windows
A note on the team wiki's incident page
blocks.explain: The code check makes the violation impossible, the test keeps the check from being removed, and the eval case watches whether the agent still tries. A prompt paragraph makes the mistake rarer without preventing it, and a wiki note runs nowhere.

blocks.prompt: Think of your last bug that took more than an hour. What was your first guess, and what evidence would have ruled it out in five minutes?
blocks.answer: There is no single right answer. A good one names the first guess and a cheap check that would have cleared or confirmed it, such as a status code, one trace, a cache bypass, or failures grouped by type. Then make that check the first step next time.

fieldGuide.symptom: "The model got worse" right after a change to infrastructure, a job, or a config
causes: Infrastructure errors graded as wrong answers
Retrieval or tool data changed underneath the model
fieldGuide.look: Eval failures grouped by error type and by retrieval outcome, and the change log for the same window.
fieldGuide.confirm: New failures cluster on timeouts, tool errors, or missing retrieval, or in a time window that matches a job or deploy.
fieldGuide.fix: Fix the infrastructure, then compare versions on a frozen setup. Reruns cost time and API spend.

fieldGuide.symptom: Answers stay stale after the help-center content was updated
causes: A response cache whose key ignores content version
A re-index that failed or skipped the article
fieldGuide.look: The trace for one stale answer: was there a cache hit, a retrieval span, an LLM span?
fieldGuide.confirm: A cache hit with no retrieval or LLM span, or retrieved chunks with an old updated time.
fieldGuide.fix: Tie cache invalidation to content changes. Shorter TTLs help but cost hit ratio.

fieldGuide.symptom: Customer charged or refunded twice; the agent trajectory shows one tool call
causes: A queue redelivered a job after a worker died before acknowledging
A client or proxy retried a non-idempotent request
fieldGuide.look: Worker logs for the job ID, and pod events around the time.
fieldGuide.confirm: The same job ID runs on two workers, with a crash or OOMKilled between.
fieldGuide.fix: Idempotency keys on the side effect, and a unique constraint as a backstop.

fieldGuide.symptom: LLM cost per ticket jumped while error rate and quality look unchanged
causes: Client timeouts shorter than generations, retried and billed
fieldGuide.look: Calls, input tokens, cached tokens, and output tokens per ticket, by step and attempt.
fieldGuide.confirm: Attempts per call or calls per ticket rose, or cached input tokens fell to near zero.
fieldGuide.fix: Fit timeouts to the longest allowed output, cap retries, and keep changing content out of the prompt prefix.

fieldGuide.symptom: 502s for a minute or two during every deploy, including a redeploy of the same image
causes: Pods exit before in-flight requests finish and before routing stops sending traffic
fieldGuide.look: nginx error log lines at deploy time and pod shutdown timing after SIGTERM.
fieldGuide.confirm: Upstream 'connection refused' or 'prematurely closed' errors coincide with pods exiting within a second of SIGTERM.
fieldGuide.fix: Graceful shutdown with a short pre-stop delay, within the termination grace period.

fieldGuide.symptom: Agent repeats an action it already completed until it hits the turn limit
causes: A follow-up read hits a lagging replica
The tool result does not state what was done
fieldGuide.look: The trajectory turn by turn, then the same rows on the primary and the replica.
fieldGuide.confirm: The write exists on the primary while the agent's read showed the old state.
fieldGuide.fix: Read-your-writes for the agent's session and tool results that return the new record.

fieldGuide.symptom: A fix made the symptom disappear and nobody can explain why
causes: A cache, retry, or queue is masking the fault
A second change happened at the same time
fieldGuide.look: Retry counts, cache hit ratio, and queue redelivery counts before and after.
fieldGuide.confirm: The underlying failure count is unchanged, only hidden.
fieldGuide.fix: Remove the mask in a test environment and reproduce, then fix the cause and keep the metric that exposed it.

fieldGuide.symptom: Eval failures begin exactly one hour into the run with 401 errors
causes: A service token fetched once at startup expired
fieldGuide.look: The first 401's time relative to the harness start, and the token lifetime.
fieldGuide.confirm: Failures start at the token's lifetime and every later tool call fails.
fieldGuide.fix: Refresh tokens before expiry, and report infrastructure errors separately from graded failures.

glossary.def: How many users, requests, or records a failure or a change can affect. Canaries, flags, and limits exist to shrink it.
Halving the space of suspects with each experiment: over commits, layers, config, data, or time.
An action that stops harm during an incident, such as a rollback, flag, or limit, without necessarily fixing the cause.
The fault that, once fixed, prevents the incident from recurring. Incidents often also have contributing factors that made it worse or slower to find.
A cache, retry, queue, or fallback hiding a fault so the symptom shrinks or moves while the fault stays.
Two or more changes shipped together, so an effect cannot be attributed to either without separating them.
Two versions of code, schema, model, or index running at once, such as during a rollout, and disagreeing about data or behavior.
A guarantee that after you write, your own later reads see the write. Breaks when reads go to a lagging replica or cache.
A unique ID sent with a request so the receiver performs the action once even if the request arrives several times.
A written account of an incident: timeline, cause, impact, why detection took as long as it did, and specific actions. Blameless by design.
A personal log of each hunt: symptom, first guess, evidence, actual cause, and time lost to wrong guesses.
A recorded task added to the eval set after a failure, so later versions are checked against that failure every run.

apply.title: Write a postmortem and a guard for your last real bug
steps: Pick the last bug in your own project that took more than an hour. Write its timeline in five lines.
Classify the symptom as error, slow, wrong, intermittent, or costly, and name the layer where the fault was born.
Write down your first guess and the cheapest check that would have ruled it in or out.
Add one guard that runs, a test, an eval case, or an alert, and confirm it fails against the old behavior.

quiz.context: On Monday the store stopped offering free return shipping and updated the help-center article. On Wednesday, Relay still answers "Is return shipping free?" with yes. Asked "Do I have to pay to send an item back?", it correctly says the customer pays. The nightly re-index job succeeded both nights.
quiz.q: What is the most likely cause?
options: The vector index still holds the old shipping article
The model's training data overrides the retrieved article
A cached answer, keyed on question text, from before the change
A read replica is two days behind the primary
quiz.explain: The rephrased question gets the new answer, so the index and retrieval are current. Only the exact old wording fails, which is the signature of a response cache keyed on question text. The tempting answer, a stale index, would mislead both phrasings.
why: A stale index would give the old answer to the rephrased question too.
The model uses the retrieved article correctly for the rephrased question.
Two days of replica lag would be an outage noticed everywhere, and would also affect both phrasings.

quiz.context: After max_tokens for ticket summaries was raised, some summary requests fail. The summary endpoint waits for the full LLM response before replying.

artifact.title: nginx access log
artifact.code:
10:14:07 "POST /tickets/9921/summary" 200 rt=11.204 upstream_rt=11.201
10:14:31 "POST /tickets/9925/summary" 504 rt=60.001 upstream_rt=60.000
10:15:02 "POST /tickets/9930/summary" 200 rt=24.877 upstream_rt=24.875
10:15:40 "POST /tickets/9934/summary" 504 rt=60.002 upstream_rt=60.001

options: The LLM provider rate-limited the longer requests
nginx stopped waiting at its 60-second limit during long generations
The API crashed on long summaries and nginx relayed it
Clients gave up after a minute and nginx logged it
quiz.explain: A 504 is a gateway that waited for its upstream and gave up. Both failures sit at exactly 60 seconds, the mark of a configured timeout, while successes finish under it. Longer outputs now take longer than the proxy allows; stream the response or align the timeouts.
why: A rate limit returns 429 quickly, not after exactly 60 seconds.
A crash shows up as a 502 or a 500, not as a wait that ends at a round number.
nginx logs a client that disconnects with its own code, 499, not 504.

quiz.context: A customer submitted the same refund request twice, one second apart, and two agent runs started. Each called `lookup_order`, saw no refund, and called `issue_refund`. Both lookups ran before either refund was written. The order was refunded twice.
quiz.q: What is the underlying bug, and the fix?
options: The model ignored its instruction; make the prompt stronger
Replica lag hid the first refund; read from the primary
The queue delivered one job twice; use at-most-once delivery
A check-then-act race; enforce one refund per order in the database
quiz.explain: Two runs checked, both saw nothing, both acted: a classic check-then-act race from Day 10, now with an agent in the loop. Only a database guard such as a unique constraint or an idempotency key closes it. Each agent followed its instructions correctly.
why: Each agent did check first, as instructed; the race happens between the check and the act.
Both lookups ran before either write, so there was nothing for lag to hide.
Two agent runs made two separate calls; this is not one job delivered twice.

quiz.context: The agent's `search_help_center` tool has grown slower for months as the help_chunks table grew, and now often hits the tool timeout.

artifact.title: EXPLAIN ANALYZE for the retrieval query
artifact.code:
Limit  (actual time=3812.4..3812.5 rows=5 loops=1)
  ->  Sort  (actual time=3812.4..3812.4 rows=5 loops=1)
        Sort Key: ((embedding <=> $1))
        Sort Method: top-N heapsort
        ->  Seq Scan on help_chunks  (actual time=0.02..3101.7 rows=1840000 loops=1)
Execution Time: 3812.6 ms

options: The query embedding takes several seconds to compute
Every query computes distance to all 1.8 million chunks
The connection pool is exhausted and queries are queuing
The LLM takes too long to read the retrieved chunks
quiz.explain: A sequential scan over 1.8 million rows followed by a sort on vector distance means no approximate nearest neighbor index is used, so cost grows with the table (Days 9 and 25). Embedding, pool waits, and LLM time all happen outside this plan's execution time.
why: The query vector arrives as a parameter; its computation is not part of this plan.
Pool waits happen before the query starts and would not appear in execution time.
The LLM is not involved in the database query at all.

quiz.context: Relay's LLM spend rose 40 percent overnight with the same traffic. The only change was a deploy that puts the current date and time at the very top of the system prompt. Usage logs show cached input tokens fell to near zero.
options: The longer prompt moved requests to a pricier tier
The model writes longer answers now that it knows the date
A changing prefix means prompt caching never finds a match
Providers turn off caching for prompts that contain dates
quiz.explain: Prompt caching reuses work for an identical prompt prefix. A timestamp at the top makes every prefix unique, so every request pays full input price. Moving changing content to the end restores the cache. Longer answers would show in output tokens, not in cached input tokens.
why: A few added tokens do not explain a 40 percent jump, and cached tokens falling to zero points elsewhere.
Longer answers would raise output tokens; the evidence is about cached input tokens.
Caching depends on matching prefixes, not on what the content says.

quiz.q: Relay's worker calls the payment API to issue a refund, and the call sometimes times out. Which of these must be in place before retrying it automatically? Select all that apply.
options: An idempotency key the payment API honors
Exponential backoff with jitter between attempts
A cap on the number of attempts
Retrying immediately so the customer waits less
Retrying 400 validation errors the same way
Letting the agent call issue_refund again instead
quiz.explain: A timeout does not say whether the refund happened, so only an idempotency key makes a retry safe. Backoff with jitter and a cap keep retries from turning a slow dependency into a retry storm. Immediate retries add load, a 400 will fail again, and a second agent call is an unkeyed retry.

quiz.q: Put the steps of the master debugging procedure in order.
items: State the symptom precisely: expected, actual, since when
Ask what changed: code, config, data, model, schedule
Find which hop emitted the error or held the time
Follow one request by its ID through logs and traces
Test one hypothesis by bypassing, pinning, or replaying
Mitigate, fix the cause, and add a guard that runs
quiz.explain: Each step narrows the search before the next one spends effort. The change log comes before tracing because it is cheaper and often decisive. Mitigation can move earlier when harm is ongoing, but the fix and guard come only after a hypothesis is confirmed.

quiz.q: Match each Relay symptom to the most likely cause.
pairs: Pods exiting before in-flight requests finish
Saved address shows the old value on refresh
A read from a lagging replica
Same tool call repeated until the turn limit
A tool result that hides that the action succeeded
Eval drop where failed cases show timeouts
Infrastructure failures graded as wrong answers
Fluent answer citing an article deleted last week
A stale index or a cached response
quiz.explain: Each symptom names a layer if you ask which component last touched the data or the request. Notice that three of the five involve the AI half of Relay yet are caused by classic backend parts: state, timeouts, and caches.

quiz.context: Relay's nightly eval started at 01:00. The harness fetches a service token once at startup to call the internal tools API.

artifact.title: eval harness
artifact.code:
01:02:11 case=88  tool=lookup_order  status=200
01:58:40 case=241 tool=lookup_order  status=200
02:00:03 case=242 tool=lookup_order  status=401 error="token expired"
02:00:05 case=243 tool=issue_refund  status=401 error="token expired"
02:14:52 summary pass=196 fail=104 total=300

quiz.q: What is the best explanation for the failures after 02:00?
options: The tools API began rate-limiting the harness
The model started sending malformed tool arguments
The orders database went down at 02:00
The one-hour service token expired and was never refreshed
quiz.explain: A 401 with 'token expired' exactly one hour into the run is a token lifetime problem in the harness (Days 15 and 27). Those 104 failures say nothing about the model, and the score should be reported with them separated as infrastructure errors.
why: A rate limit returns 429, not 401 with 'token expired'.
Malformed arguments return 400 or 422, and would not start at a round hour.
A database outage gives 5xx errors from the tools API.

quiz.context: Relay scaled its API from one pod to four. Since then, the agent often forgets the earlier part of a conversation on a follow-up message, about three times in four. Redis memory is at 30 percent with no evictions.
quiz.q: What is the most likely cause?
options: Conversation history is kept in each API process's memory
The model's context window is too small for the history
Redis is evicting conversation keys under memory pressure
The load balancer strips the session cookie
quiz.explain: Forgetting about three times in four matches the chance of landing on one of the three other pods. Redis shows no evictions, and context size would not depend on pod count. Move conversation state to Redis or Postgres; sticky sessions would reduce it but lose history whenever a pod restarts.
why: Context limits do not change with the number of pods, and the problem began with scaling.
Redis reports no evictions and has plenty of memory.
A stripped cookie would break every request, not three in four.

quiz.q: Relay's refund step moves money and must follow policy exactly. Which design fits that requirement best?
options: The agent decides freely, guided by refund rules in the prompt
Code enforces refund rules; the model reads and proposes
A higher temperature so the agent adapts to unusual cases
A larger model with no extra checks, since it follows rules better
quiz.explain: Money and exact policy put this step on the determinism side of the ledger. The model can read the request and propose an action, but code it cannot argue with should enforce the rule. Prompt rules and bigger models make violations rarer, not impossible.
why: Prompt rules lower the rate of violations without preventing them.
Higher temperature increases variation, the opposite of what exact policy needs.
A better model still makes some mistakes, and nothing would catch them.

quiz.context: Finance reports that duplicate refunds are happening right now, a few per hour. The cause is unknown.
options: Read the worker code until you find the bug
Add a prompt instruction telling the agent never to refund twice
Pause automatic refunds with a flag and route them to human approval
Wait for tonight's eval run to measure how often it happens
quiz.explain: Mitigate first, then diagnose (Day 21). A flag that pauses the money-moving step stops the harm in minutes and buys time to find the cause. Reading code while refunds continue lets damage grow, and a prompt change guesses at a cause that may sit in the queue.
why: Harm continues while you read, and the cause may not be in that code.
It guesses that the agent is at fault, and the duplicates may come from the queue.
The eval measures recorded tickets, not today's live duplicates, and waiting extends the harm.

quiz.context: Relay's eval pass rate fell from 85 to 79 percent on the night two changes shipped: the LLM was upgraded to a new version, and the agent's tool timeout was lowered from 20 seconds to 8.
quiz.q: Describe how you would separate the effects of the two changes.
rubric: Groups failures by type first: tool timeouts and errors versus completed but graded wrong
Checks whether new failures involve tool calls running near the 8-second limit
Isolates each change: new model with the old timeout, and old model with the new timeout
Judges whether differences exceed run-to-run noise, with repeated trials or enough cases
Assesses model quality only on cases that completed under both setups
quiz.model: First I would split the new failures into tool timeouts or errors and cases that completed but were graded wrong. If many hit the 8-second limit, the timeout is a cause regardless of the model. Then I would run the new model with the old timeout and the old model with the new timeout, with repeated trials, and compare pass rates only on completed cases. That shows each change's effect separately.

quiz.context: Customers say Relay's replies got slow this afternoon. The team suspects the LLM provider. This is the trace for one slow reply.

artifact.code:
POST /tickets/7712/reply                9.84 s
  auth.verify_session                    2 ms
  db.pool.acquire                     6.91 s
  pgvector search_help_center           38 ms
  llm.generate (stream)               2.71 s
  db.insert message                     12 ms

options: Most of the time went to waiting for a database connection
The LLM provider is the main source of the slowdown
The vector search needs an approximate nearest neighbor index
Session verification is blocking the event loop
quiz.explain: Seven of the ten seconds are spent acquiring a connection from the pool, before any query runs. The LLM span is a normal few seconds and the search itself takes 38 ms. Look for what is holding connections: a slow query elsewhere, a leak, or too small a pool (Days 3, 7, and 9).
why: The LLM span is under 3 seconds of the nearly 10; it is not the main cost.
The search query itself finished in 38 ms once it had a connection.
Session verification took 2 ms.

quiz.context: Relay's behavior on refund conversations changed last Wednesday with no deploy, no prompt change, and no data change. Relay calls the model by an alias instead of a dated version.
quiz.q: What is the most likely cause, and the lasting fix?
options: The alias moved to a new model; pin a dated version and upgrade via evals
A library updated on its own; rebuild the image from scratch
The provider got slower; add timeouts and retries
Temperature drifted upward; set it explicitly again
quiz.explain: An alias can point at a new model version without any change on your side, which is the LLM version of deploying 'latest' (Days 20 and 24). Pin a dated version and treat each upgrade like a deploy, gated by evals. A running image does not change its libraries without a deploy.
why: A running container's libraries do not change without a new image being deployed.
Slowness changes latency, not the behavior of answers.
Temperature is a request parameter; it does not drift unless your code changes it.

drills.title: Relay quotes last week's refund window
drills.brief: On Tuesday the store cut its refund window from 30 to 14 days and updated the help-center article that morning. Today, Thursday, three customers were told by Relay that they had 30 days. The nightly re-index job reports success for both nights. A teammate wants to re-embed every article and add the new window to the system prompt.

steps.q: What do you do first?
options: Re-embed all help-center articles and rebuild the index
Pull the trace for one of the wrong replies by its request ID
Add the 14-day window to the system prompt
Lower the temperature to 0 for refund questions
steps.explain: One trace shows which layers actually produced the answer, which halves the search for free. Re-embedding and prompt edits are fixes for causes nobody has confirmed, and the prompt edit would hide the real fault for this one fact only.
steps.reveal: The trace for ticket 88213 shows a Redis hit and no retrieval or LLM spans. The reply took 14 ms.

artifact.code:
POST /tickets/88213/reply              14 ms
  auth.verify_session                  1 ms
  redis GET ans:v2:9f3c1e...           2 ms   HIT
  render_reply                         3 ms

steps.q: What does that trace tell you?
options: Retrieval returned the old version of the article
The model ignored the updated article in its context
The answer came from the response cache, so retrieval and the model never ran
The re-index job failed silently on Tuesday night
steps.explain: With no retrieval span and no LLM span, neither ran for this reply. The answer was written into the cache earlier and served again. Whether the index is fresh is a separate question this trace cannot answer.
steps.reveal: Keys under `ans:v2:` are a hash of the normalized question text, with a 7-day TTL. The entry for this question was written on Monday, before the article changed.

steps.q: Before fixing the cache, what do you verify?
options: That a request bypassing the cache gets the 14-day answer
That Redis has enough free memory
That the model version has not changed this week
That nginx is not caching responses as well
steps.explain: There may be two faults. A cache-bypassed request tests the index, retrieval, and model together. If it is right, the cache is the only problem; if it is wrong, the re-index needs attention too.
steps.reveal: With the cache bypassed, Relay retrieves the refund chunk updated on Tuesday at 09:12 and answers 14 days. The index is current.

steps.q: What is the durable fix?
options: Flush all of Redis every night right after the re-index runs
Turn the response cache off entirely for every question
Shorten the answer cache TTL from seven days to one hour
Invalidate cached answers when the re-index changes a source article
steps.explain: The cache must forget answers when the content behind them changes. Flushing all of Redis would also wipe sessions and rate-limit counters. A one-hour TTL narrows the window but keeps it, and disabling the cache gives up its cost savings to fix a keying problem.
steps.reveal: The cache now records which articles each answer used, and the re-index deletes those entries when an article changes.

drills.debrief: Root cause: a response cache keyed only on question text kept serving an answer written before the policy changed, and nothing tied invalidation to content updates. The index and model were fine, and the obvious fixes (re-embedding, prompt edits) would have changed nothing. A trace with a cache-hit marker found it in minutes. Days 7, 12, and 25 meet here: every answer path needs to record whether the model ran at all.

drills.title: The eval dropped the night the prompt changed
drills.brief: Relay's nightly eval fell from 84 to 76 percent. Two changes landed yesterday: system prompt v14, shorter and reorganized, and an ops change that moved the nightly help-center re-index job from 01:00 to 02:30 to avoid the database backup. The eval runs from 02:00 to about 03:10. The prompt author is preparing a revert.

steps.q: What do you do first?
options: Revert to prompt v13 and rerun the eval
Rerun the eval unchanged to check for noise
Read ten failing transcripts chosen at random
Group the new failures by retrieval outcome and by time
steps.explain: Two changes shipped together, so the first job is to see which one the failures follow. The harness logs retrieved chunks and timestamps, so grouping is free. Reverting first would confound the result further, and a rerun costs an hour without saying why.
steps.reveal: Of 31 new failures, 24 retrieved nothing from the expected article, and all 24 ran between 02:31 and 02:52. Cases before 02:30 fail at last week's rate.

steps.q: What do you check next?
options: The provider's status page for an outage at 02:30
What ran against the database between 02:30 and 02:55
Whether the grader changed this week
Redis memory and eviction counts overnight
steps.explain: The failures are retrieval misses confined to a time window. Something changed the help_chunks table during that window. A provider outage would show errors, not empty retrieval, and the grader cannot make retrieval return nothing.
steps.reveal: The re-index job ran from 02:30 to 02:54, overlapping the eval for the first time because of yesterday's schedule change.

steps.q: Why would re-indexing make articles vanish from retrieval?
options: The embedding API returned errors for some articles
The vector index was rebuilt and unusable until it finished
Replica lag hid the newly inserted chunks
Old chunks are deleted and committed minutes before new ones are inserted
steps.explain: The log shows each article's delete committed on its own, then minutes of embedding, then the insert. Anyone reading in between sees no chunks for that article. That is Day 10's atomicity problem inside a Day 25 pipeline.

artifact.title: reindex job
artifact.code:
02:31:04 article=refund-policy   DELETE 14 chunks   COMMIT
02:31:05 article=refund-policy   embedding 15 chunks
02:33:40 article=refund-policy   INSERT 15 chunks   COMMIT
02:33:41 article=shipping-times  DELETE 9 chunks    COMMIT
02:33:42 article=shipping-times  embedding 9 chunks
02:35:58 article=shipping-times  INSERT 9 chunks    COMMIT

steps.q: What is the right fix for the job?
options: Embed first, then delete old chunks and insert new ones in one transaction
Move the job back to 01:00 and leave the code alone
Have retrieval retry once when it finds nothing
Pause the eval while the job is running
steps.explain: Doing the slow embedding first and the swap in one transaction means readers see either the old chunks or the new ones, never none. Moving the job back only hides it from the eval; customers asking at 01:00 still hit the same gaps.
steps.reveal: With the swap made atomic and the eval rerun, retrieval misses drop back to last week's level.

steps.q: How do you now judge prompt v14 on its own?
options: Accept last night's 76 percent as v14's score
Revert v14 anyway, since it shipped on a bad night
Run v13 and v14 on the same index snapshot, with repeated trials
Compare only the cases that passed on both nights
steps.explain: A fair comparison holds everything except the prompt fixed, and repeats enough to see past noise. Last night's score measured the re-index, and comparing only cases that passed both nights hides every regression.
steps.reveal: On a frozen snapshot, v13 scores 84 percent and v14 scores 85 percent across three trials each, a difference within noise.

drills.debrief: Two changes shipped together and the visible one, the prompt, was blamed. The real cause was a schedule change that made a non-atomic re-index overlap the eval, which also exposed a production bug: any customer asking during re-indexing got no retrieval. Grouping failures by retrieval outcome and time found it. The guards: an atomic swap, an eval that waits for the re-index and records the index version, and one change at a time.

drills.title: Some customers were refunded twice
drills.brief: Finance found 23 duplicate refunds last week, all on tickets Relay handled. The agent's `issue_refund` tool enqueues a refund job, and a worker calls the payment provider. Last week the agent prompt gained a line asking it to confirm each refund. Since this morning, refunds need human approval as a stopgap, so no new duplicates are being created.

steps.q: With the harm stopped, what do you check first?
options: Revert last week's prompt line about confirming refunds
Count `issue_refund` calls in the duplicated tickets' trajectories
Restart the worker fleet to clear any stuck state
Add a deduplication step to finance's reconciliation
steps.explain: The obvious suspect is the agent calling twice after the prompt change. The trajectories confirm or clear it in minutes. Reverting first would test only one theory and leave you guessing if duplicates continue.
steps.reveal: In all 23 tickets the agent called `issue_refund` exactly once. Each job ID appears twice in the worker logs.

steps.q: What do these worker logs show?
options: The agent enqueued two jobs that share an ID
The payment API retried the refund internally
Worker-7 refunded but never acknowledged, so the job was redelivered
Two workers pulled the same job at once due to a broker bug
steps.explain: Worker-7 called the payment API and never reached the acknowledgement. After the visibility timeout the broker handed the job to worker-2, as at-least-once delivery promises. The 30-second gap matches a timeout, not a simultaneous pull.

artifact.code:
10:41:02 worker-7 job=rf_5521 start order=88412 amount=39.00
10:41:03 worker-7 job=rf_5521 payment_api ok refund_id=re_9QK
10:41:03 worker-7 job=rf_5521 refund row committed
10:41:33 worker-2 job=rf_5521 start order=88412 amount=39.00 (redelivered)
10:41:34 worker-2 job=rf_5521 payment_api ok refund_id=re_A7T
10:41:34 worker-2 job=rf_5521 ack

steps.reveal: Pod events show worker-7 was OOMKilled at 10:41:04. Memory on refund workers climbs during a nightly batch and several were killed last week.

steps.q: Which fix stops duplicates no matter why a worker dies?
options: Raise the memory limit on refund workers
Switch the queue to at-most-once delivery
Acknowledge the job before calling the payment API
Send an idempotency key derived from the job ID to the payment API
steps.explain: Workers will die for many reasons, so the side effect itself must be safe to repeat. With the key, a redelivered job gets the original refund back. At-most-once delivery and early acks trade duplicate refunds for lost ones, and more memory fixes only this crash cause.
steps.reveal: The payment provider supports idempotency keys. A replayed job now returns the original refund ID instead of creating a new one.

steps.q: What would have caught this before finance did?
options: A unique constraint on refunds per job, plus an alert on redeliveries
Running the nightly eval twice as often
Logging every agent message at debug level
A larger model that confirms refunds more carefully
steps.explain: The database would have rejected the second refund row, and a redelivery alert would have pointed at the dying workers. The eval and the agent logs were never going to see it, because the agent behaved correctly.
steps.reveal: The OOM is tracked separately; with the key and constraint in place, it now causes a delay instead of a double refund.

drills.debrief: The agent was the obvious suspect and was innocent. A worker killed for memory after charging and before acknowledging let the queue redeliver the job, and the payment call was not idempotent. Days 17, 18, 21, and 26 meet here. The fix was an idempotency key on the side effect and a unique constraint as a backstop. The general lesson: an agent tool that reaches money through a queue inherits every at-least-once duplicate.

drills.title: The LLM bill tripled and nothing errored
drills.brief: Relay's LLM bill for Tuesday is three times Monday's. Ticket volume is flat, the error rate is the usual 0.2 percent, and the eval pass rate is unchanged. Monday afternoon's deploy raised max_tokens for replies from 600 to 1500 so long answers stop being cut off. A teammate assumes longer answers explain the cost and wants to lower it back.

steps.q: What do you gather first?
options: Lower max_tokens back to 600 and watch tomorrow's bill
Ask the provider whether prices changed on Tuesday
Switch replies to a smaller, cheaper model
Break cost down into calls, attempts, and tokens per ticket
steps.explain: Cost is calls times tokens per call. Splitting it shows whether answers got longer or calls multiplied, and the two need different fixes. Reverting max_tokens brings back truncation and tests only one theory.
steps.reveal: Output tokens per request rose about 30 percent. The provider's usage export shows billed requests per call rose from 1.02 to 2.4.

artifact.title: app metrics and provider usage export
artifact.code:
metric                     monday   tuesday
llm_calls_per_ticket         2.1      2.1
billed_requests_per_call     1.02     2.4
out_tokens_per_request       410      530
error_rate                   0.2%     0.2%

steps.q: What explains the extra attempts?
options: The provider is rate limiting and the client retries the 429s
Long generations hit the 30 s client timeout and are retried
The agent loop is repeating its tool calls more often
Prompt caching stopped matching after Monday's deploy
steps.explain: The log shows client-side timeouts at exactly 30 seconds, then a retry. The usage export shows the abandoned attempts were still generated and billed, so a client timeout did not stop the cost. Calls per ticket are flat, which clears the agent loop.

artifact.code:
11:02:14 llm ticket=7781 attempt=1 client timeout after 30.0s
11:02:45 llm ticket=7781 attempt=2 client timeout after 30.0s
11:03:09 llm ticket=7781 attempt=3 ok 23.6s out_tokens=1120

steps.q: Why did the error rate not move?
options: Errors are sampled and the sample missed these
Timeouts are logged at info level instead of error
Retries eventually succeeded, so the failures turned into cost and latency
The eval harness absorbed the failures
steps.explain: Output length varies from sample to sample, so a later attempt often finishes under 30 seconds. The retry hid every failure from the error rate and moved it into the bill and into p95 latency. This is masking.
steps.reveal: Reply latency p95 rose from 14 to 58 seconds on Tuesday. Nobody alerted on it.

steps.q: What is the right fix?
options: Stream replies and set the timeout to fit the longest allowed output
Lower max_tokens back to 600 so generations finish in time
Raise the retry limit to five so more calls succeed
Move replies to a cheaper model to offset the retries
steps.explain: The timeout has to fit the work you now ask for, and streaming shows progress so a long generation is not mistaken for a hung one. Reverting max_tokens brings back truncation, and more retries or a cheaper model pay for the same mistake differently.
steps.reveal: With streaming and a timeout sized for 1500 tokens, attempts per call return to about 1.0 and cost per ticket rises only by the longer outputs.

drills.debrief: Raising max_tokens made some generations longer than a client timeout nobody revisited. Each timed-out attempt was retried and billed, and eventual success hid it from the error rate. Days 18, 24, and 13 meet here. The fix was streaming with a timeout sized to the longest allowed output. Alert on cost per ticket, attempts per call, and p95 latency, not only errors, because retries turn errors into cost.

drills.title: A burst of 502s during every deploy
drills.brief: Since Relay's API moved to Kubernetes, every deploy brings one to two minutes of 502s for about 2 percent of requests. The team has reverted two recent changes on the theory that each introduced a bug, and both reverts also showed the spike. Deploys are rolling updates behind nginx.

steps.q: What do you test first?
options: Revert the most recent change and redeploy
Redeploy the current image unchanged and watch for the spike
Raise nginx's upstream timeouts
Add replicas so each pod carries less traffic
steps.explain: If a no-op redeploy reproduces the spike, the code is cleared and the deploy mechanics are the suspect. That one experiment halves the search. Another revert repeats an experiment that has already failed twice.
steps.reveal: Redeploying the same image produces the same burst of 502s.

steps.q: Which hop emits the 502, and what does it say?
options: nginx reached pods that were shutting down or already gone
The API returned 502 from its own error handler
The load balancer's TLS certificate failed to validate
Requests timed out inside the app and were reported as 502
steps.explain: These are nginx's own errors about its upstream: connections refused and connections closed mid-request. The pods it was routing to had stopped. A timeout would be a 504, and a TLS failure would never reach nginx's upstream step.

artifact.title: nginx error log at deploy time
artifact.code:
10:14:02 upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header from upstream
10:14:03 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream
10:14:04 connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream

steps.q: The old pods' logs show the timing below. What is the mechanism?
options: New pods pass readiness too slowly and the rollout stalls
A liveness probe is killing healthy pods during the deploy
Old pods exit at once while routing still sends them traffic
Image pulls on new nodes delay the rollout
steps.explain: Removing a terminating pod from routing takes a few seconds to reach every proxy. A pod that exits on SIGTERM immediately drops its in-flight requests and refuses the ones still being sent to it.

artifact.code:
10:14:02.110 SIGTERM received
10:14:02.180 shutting down, 6 requests in flight
10:14:02.240 process exited

steps.q: What is the right fix?
options: Have nginx retry every failed request on another pod
Deploy only at night when traffic is low
Raise the replica count so fewer requests hit each pod
Add a short pre-stop delay and graceful shutdown that drains in-flight requests
steps.explain: The pod should keep serving briefly while routing catches up, then finish its in-flight requests before exiting, within the termination grace period. Retrying every request in nginx would repeat non-idempotent POSTs such as replies and refunds, which is Day 2's duplicate problem.
steps.reveal: With a short pre-stop delay and graceful shutdown, the next three deploys show no 502s.

drills.debrief: Every deploy, not every change, caused the errors. Pods exited on SIGTERM before routing stopped sending them traffic, and nginx reported the refused and dropped connections as 502s. Days 2, 19, and 21 meet here. The team lost two reverts to the obvious cause because nobody ran the no-op redeploy. The general lesson: when a symptom follows an event, reproduce the event without the change before blaming the change.

drills.title: The agent keeps refunding an order it already refunded
drills.brief: Since Monday, about 4 percent of refund conversations hit the agent's 12-turn limit and escalate to a human. On Monday, ops moved `lookup_order` reads to a new Postgres read replica to offload the primary. The LLM was upgraded to a new version the week before. A teammate says the new model is confused by refunds.

steps.q: What do you do first?
options: Roll back to the previous model version
Raise the turn limit from 12 to 20
Read one escalated conversation's trajectory turn by turn
Add a prompt rule never to call `issue_refund` twice
steps.explain: One trajectory shows what the agent saw and did at every turn, which tells you whether the model or its inputs went wrong. The other options each act on an unconfirmed theory, and a longer turn limit would only make the loops cost more.
steps.reveal: The agent refunds, looks up the order, sees no refund, and tries again, receiving 409 each time.

steps.q: Which reading of the trajectory is right?
options: The refund failed, and the agent is right to retry
The model ignores tool results entirely
The 409 means the payment provider is down
The refund exists, but `lookup_order` does not show it yet
steps.explain: The 409 says the refund exists, while the lookup says it does not. Two tools disagree about the same row. The model is reacting reasonably to contradictory evidence, not ignoring it.
steps.reveal: On the primary, the refund row was created at turn 3. The replica lag graph shows 20 to 60 seconds of lag during business hours since Monday.

steps.q: What is the best fix?
options: Raise the turn limit so the agent eventually gives up on its own
Read from the primary after a write, and have `issue_refund` return the refund record
Roll back the model upgrade to see whether loops stop
Tell the agent in the prompt to trust 409 over `lookup_order`
steps.explain: Read-your-writes for the agent's session removes the contradiction at its source, and a tool result that states the outcome removes the need to verify. The prompt rule patches one symptom of stale data, which will mislead the agent in other ways.
steps.reveal: With reads pinned to the primary for 2 minutes after a write, and the refund record returned by the tool, loops stop.

steps.q: How do you make sure the model upgrade is not a second cause?
options: Roll back the model in production and watch for a week
Assume it is fine because the 409 was handled correctly
Ask the model whether the tool results confused it
Run refund evals on the new model with reads pinned to the primary
steps.explain: Holding the read path fixed and testing the new model isolates the second change. A production rollback for a week is slow and costly, and asking the model about its own reasoning is not evidence.
steps.reveal: With primary reads, the new model's loop rate is 0.1 percent, the same as the old model before Monday.

drills.debrief: The model was blamed, and the cause was replica lag. After writing the refund on the primary, the agent read the order from a replica that had not caught up, saw no refund, and tried again. Days 11, 26, and 6 meet here. The fix was read-your-writes for the agent and tool results that report what they did. The general lesson: an agent acts on what its tools tell it, so stale reads become wrong actions.
